char.peterloo_crowd: The Crowd at St Peter's Field
level.arthur_sword.fact: The legend goes: at the New Year's tournament, Sir Kay left his sword at the inn and sent his young squire Arthur to fetch it. The house was locked, and Arthur, not wanting to return empty-handed, simply pulled the sword from the stone by the church. Kay recognized the blade and told his father, Sir Ector, that he had drawn it himself — but Ector made him swear on the Bible, and Kay confessed. The sword was set back in the stone, and Arthur drew it again at Candlemas, at Easter and at Pentecost, until the barons gave in. Then Merlin revealed the truth: the boy was the son of Uther and Igraine, secretly given to Ector to raise. The sword in the stone is not Excalibur — that one the Lady of the Lake would give Arthur later. Whether a "historical Arthur" ever existed, a British war leader fighting the Saxons around 500, is still hotly debated.
level.arthur_sword.goal: An unknown squire draws the sword from the stone, Merlin reveals the secret of his birth — and Arthur becomes king
level.arthur_sword.hint: First the sword, then the secret, then the crown. The foster brother is always close by — and he will like that sword very much.
level.arthur_sword.intro: King Uther Pendragon has died without an acknowledged heir, and the barons of Britain are tearing the land apart. At Christmas, a stone with an anvil appeared by a London church, and in it a sword bearing the words: "Whoso pulleth out this sword of this stone and anvil is rightwise king born of all England." Hundreds of knights have tugged at it — the sword has not budged.
level.arthur_sword.source: Thomas Malory, 'Le Morte d'Arthur' (1485), Book I; Robert de Boron, 'Merlin' (c. 1200)
level.arthur_sword.title: The Sword in the Stone
level.augustine_597.fact: Bede tells us that Gregory conceived the mission after seeing fair-haired slave boys in a Roman market: "Not Angles, but angels." King Æthelberht met Augustine on the Isle of Thanet — in the open air, so that the foreigners could not bewitch him indoors. He replied that he would not abandon the faith of his fathers at once, but he allowed them to preach and gave the monks lodgings in Canterbury. Soon the king was baptized — probably in St Martin's Church, where Bertha prayed. According to Bede, Æthelberht forced no one: he simply loved those who were baptized all the more. Augustine became the first Archbishop of Canterbury. The conversion of England took nearly a century: paganism kept coming back, and Irish and Scottish monks in the north baptized by their own customs — a dispute settled at the Synod of Whitby in 664.
level.augustine_597.goal: The monk Augustine, sent by the Pope, preaches to the King of Kent — and Æthelberht is baptized without forcing anyone to follow him
level.augustine_597.hint: A pagan king fears sorcery, and walls help it work. The queen is already a Christian — you can't do without her. And remember: Æthelberht compelled no one.
level.augustine_597.intro: The year 597. Roman Britain fell long ago, and the east of the island is ruled by the pagan kingdoms of the Angles and Saxons. Pope Gregory the Great sends Prior Augustine with forty monks to distant Kent. The monks are so afraid of the barbarians that they nearly turn back on the way. Their hope is Queen Bertha of Kent, a Christian Frankish princess who prays in the old Roman church of St Martin.
level.augustine_597.source: Bede, 'Ecclesiastical History of the English People' (731), Books I–II
level.augustine_597.title: A Door into Kent
level.bannockburn_1314.fact: On June 23, the first day, the English knight Henry de Bohun spotted the King of Scots on a small horse in front of his lines and charged at him with a lance. Bruce dodged and with a single blow of his axe split Bohun's helmet and skull — and afterwards regretted only his broken axe-shaft. That same day the spearmen of Thomas Randolph, Earl of Moray, formed into a bristling schiltron and drove off the English cavalry. On June 24 the Scots went on the attack themselves, and the English army, which had camped for the night between the Bannock Burn and the marshes, was trapped; many drowned. Edward II fled to Dunbar and from there by sea to England. The war did not end there: the Declaration of Arbroath of 1320 proclaimed Scotland's independence, and England recognized it only in the treaty of 1328. The film "Braveheart" gets much of this wrong — Wallace had been executed back in 1305.
level.bannockburn_1314.goal: Bruce kills the knight de Bohun in single combat, Randolph's schiltrons hold firm — and Edward II's army, pinned against the burn, flees
level.bannockburn_1314.hint: In the open field the English cavalry is stronger. Victory lies where the ground helps the weaker side — and the first to charge the King of Scots is the knight himself.
level.bannockburn_1314.intro: June 1314. For eight years Robert the Bruce, crowned King of Scots, has been winning back castles from the English. The last large English garrison is at Stirling, and its commander has promised to surrender if no relief arrives by Midsummer Day. King Edward II is marching to its rescue with a huge army and heavy cavalry. Bruce is outnumbered several times over.
level.bannockburn_1314.source: John Barbour, 'The Brus' (1375); 'Vita Edwardi Secundi' (The Life of Edward II)
level.bannockburn_1314.title: Bannockburn
level.black_death_1348.fact: In a year and a half the plague killed, by various estimates, between a third and a half of England's people. Canterbury alone saw three archbishops in a single year: two died of the pestilence, and in 1349 Simon Islip took the see. Henry Knighton, a canon of Leicester, wrote that sheep wandered the fields without shepherds, there was no one to bring in the harvest, and reapers demanded three times their old wage. In June 1349 the king issued the Ordinance of Labourers: wages could be paid only "as before the pestilence," and every able-bodied man without land was bound to work for whoever called on him. In 1350 Islip, in his letter "Effrenata," thundered against priests who charged three times as much for requiem masses. In 1351 the ordinance became the Statute of Labourers. Wages could not be frozen, and resentment of these laws exploded thirty years later in Wat Tyler's revolt.
level.black_death_1348.goal: The plague mows down England, the surviving workers demand more — and the king and the Church try to force back the old prices
level.black_death_1348.hint: Don't go out to meet the ship from Gascony. First the pestilence and the shortage of hands, then the king's decree, and the Church follows after.
level.black_death_1348.intro: Summer 1348. A ship from Gascony docks at the port of Melcombe in Dorset — and brings the plague that has already ravaged Italy and France. Medicine is powerless: physicians talk of "bad air" and the conjunction of planets. King Edward III is in the thick of his war with France, and his daughter Joan has just died of the plague in Bordeaux on her way to her bridegroom.
level.black_death_1348.source: Henry Knighton, 'Chronicle' (late 14th c.); Ordinance of Labourers (1349); Simon Islip's letter 'Effrenata' (1350)
level.black_death_1348.title: The Black Death
level.boer_1900.fact: The war began in October 1899. In June 1900 the British took Pretoria and President Paul Kruger left for Europe, but the war dragged on for two more years. The new commander, Lord Kitchener, burned farms, built networks of blockhouses and herded Boer women and children into camps. There were separate camps for Black Africans. In 1901 the Englishwoman Emily Hobhouse toured the camps and published a report on the hunger and disease; the government sent a commission headed by the suffragist Millicent Fawcett, while Hobhouse herself was refused re-entry that same year and deported. Some 28,000 Boers died in the camps, most of them children, and at least 14,000 Africans — whose deaths were the most poorly recorded. On May 31, 1902, after negotiations at Vereeniging, the peace treaty was signed in Pretoria: the republics became British colonies. Article Eight postponed the question of votes for Africans until self-government — in other words, handed it to the whites. The journalist Sol Plaatje, who had lived through the Siege of Mafeking, later became one of the founders of the African National Congress and described where all this led.
level.boer_1900.goal: Facing Boer guerrillas, Kitchener burns farms and builds camps, Emily Hobhouse tells Britain about them, and peace is made without the Africans
level.boer_1900.hint: Taking the capital is not the same as ending the war. A peace signed by white men has a third party — it simply wasn't invited.
level.boer_1900.intro: 1900, South Africa. Britain is at war with two Boer republics — the Transvaal, where the world's richest goldfields were found, and the Orange Free State. The British army takes their capitals, but the mounted commandos of General Louis Botha fight on. Between the two white armies live African communities — whom almost no one in this war asks anything.
level.boer_1900.source: Emily Hobhouse, 'The Brunt of the War and Where It Fell' (1902); Sol Plaatje, 'Native Life in South Africa' (1916); Treaty of Vereeniging (1902)
level.boer_1900.title: War for the Veld
level.boudica_60.fact: The Romans seized the kingdom, Boudica was flogged and her daughters raped. The Iceni and their neighbours the Trinovantes rose up: they burned the veterans' colony of Camulodunum, home to the hated Temple of Claudius, and then Londinium and Verulamium. Tacitus speaks of 70,000 dead — a figure that is probably exaggerated. Catus Decianus fled to Gaul. Suetonius, fresh from crushing the druids on Mona, hurried back. Somewhere along Watling Street he drew up about ten thousand legionaries in a narrow valley with a forest at their backs; the British host, which had even brought wagons full of families to the field, was routed. Boudica, according to Tacitus, took poison. The site of the battle has never been found. In the Victorian era Boudica became a symbol of Britain — her statue in a chariot stands by Westminster Bridge.
level.boudica_60.goal: The Romans plunder the kingdom of the Iceni, Queen Boudica burns three cities, and the governor Suetonius destroys her army
level.boudica_60.hint: A revolt is born of an outrage, and the man behind the outrage must see it. The governor can't be far away in the west at the hour of the decisive battle.
level.boudica_60.intro: AD 60. Prasutagus, king of the Iceni in eastern Britain, is dying. He has left half his kingdom to the Emperor Nero, hoping to keep the other half for his wife Boudica and their daughters. But Roman officials led by the procurator Catus Decianus decide to take it all. The governor, Suetonius Paulinus, is meanwhile far away, preparing an attack on the druids' island in the west.
level.boudica_60.source: Tacitus, 'Annals', Book XIV, 31–37; Tacitus, 'Agricola'; Cassius Dio, Book LXII
level.boudica_60.title: Boudica's Fire
level.chartists_1848.fact: The People's Charter was drawn up in 1838 by the cabinet-maker William Lovett and his comrades. Six points: the vote for every man over 21, the secret ballot, no property qualification for MPs, payment of MPs, equal constituencies and annual parliamentary elections. Parliament rejected the petitions of 1839 and 1842. In 1848 the government expected revolution: the old Duke of Wellington posted troops at the bridges, some 85,000 special constables were sworn in, and Queen Victoria and her family were taken off to the Isle of Wight. Somewhere between 20,000 and 150,000 people, by various estimates, gathered on Kennington Common. The police warned the Chartist leader Feargus O'Connor that a procession to Parliament would not be allowed through, and he persuaded the crowd to go home. The petition was carried in three cabs. O'Connor claimed 5.7 million signatures; the clerks counted about two million, among them "Queen Victoria," "Wellington" and "Mr Punch," and Parliament laughed it out. The movement faded, but by 1918 five of the six points had become law — all except annual elections.
level.chartists_1848.goal: For the third time the Chartists bring millions of signatures for the vote to Parliament — peacefully, in cabs, and once again they are refused
level.chartists_1848.hint: A petition without the six points is a blank sheet of paper. In 1848 the only way to reach Parliament is without the crowd.
level.chartists_1848.intro: 1848. Revolutions are sweeping Europe: Paris has overthrown its king, Vienna and Berlin are rising. In Britain only one adult man in five has the vote. The Chartists — the first mass working-class movement — call a great rally in London for April 10 to present their petition to Parliament for the third time.
level.chartists_1848.source: The People's Charter (1838); Dorothy Thompson, 'The Chartists' (1984)
level.chartists_1848.title: A Charter in the Rain
level.claudius_43.fact: Plautius defeated the Britons in a two-day battle on a river — probably the Medway: Gallic auxiliaries swam across it in full armour. Togodumnus soon fell, while Caratacus slipped away west and fought on for eight more years in the mountains of Wales, until Cartimandua, queen of the Brigantes, handed him over to the Romans. Plautius halted at the Thames and sent for the emperor. Claudius arrived with reinforcements and, according to Cassius Dio, with elephants, entered Camulodunum (Colchester), and spent just sixteen days in Britain. His triumphal arch in Rome declared that he had received the submission of eleven kings. So began the Roman province of Britannia — for almost four hundred years.
level.claudius_43.goal: The legate Plautius defeats the chieftain brothers on the river, and Emperor Claudius arrives with elephants to receive Britain's submission in person
level.claudius_43.hint: The legate wins the victory, and the emperor takes the glory. One of the brothers won't surrender — he has eight more years of war ahead.
level.claudius_43.intro: AD 43. Julius Caesar landed in Britain twice but never conquered it. Emperor Claudius, whom Rome considers a fool, needs a real victory. Four legions under Aulus Plautius cross the Channel. Facing them are the sons of the late king Cunobelinus: Caratacus and Togodumnus.
level.claudius_43.source: Cassius Dio, 'Roman History', Book LX; Tacitus, 'Annals', Book XII
level.claudius_43.title: Claudius's Eagles
level.cnut_1016.fact: On October 18, 1016, at Assandun in Essex, Eadric led his men off the field in the heat of battle, and Edmund's army was routed. The kings met on Alney Island in the River Severn and divided the country: Wessex to Edmund, the lands north of the Thames to Cnut; whoever outlived the other would get it all. Five weeks later, on November 30, Edmund died — of his wounds or, as was said later, at the hands of assassins, though there is no proof. Cnut became king of all England, and in 1017 he married Emma of Normandy, Æthelred's widow, binding himself to the old dynasty. Cnut had Eadric executed at Christmas 1017 — even his new master did not trust a traitor. Cnut later ruled Denmark and Norway as well. The story of him ordering the waves to turn back is a later parable about how a king's power is nothing before God.
level.cnut_1016.goal: The Dane Cnut wins at Assandun thanks to a traitor, divides England with Edmund, gains the whole of it and marries the former king's widow
level.cnut_1016.hint: The battle won't be decided by the Dane or the king, but by the man who leaves the field. Better to win the crown by treaty than by blood: the queen won't marry a murderer.
level.cnut_1016.intro: 1016. The Danish prince Cnut has been fighting for the English throne for more than a year. King Æthelred the Unready died in April, and England is defended by his son Edmund, known as Ironside. In his army is Eadric Streona, ealdorman of Mercia, who over his lifetime has switched from the English to the Danes and back more than once.
level.cnut_1016.title: Cnut's Crown
level.cromford_1771.fact: The Warrington clockmaker John Kay had earlier helped the loom reed-maker Thomas Highs build a spinning machine. In 1767 Arkwright hired him, and in 1769 Arkwright took out a patent on the "water frame." The money came from the hosiers Samuel Need and Jedediah Strutt. The first mill was driven by horses, and in 1771 a mill with a waterwheel started turning at Cromford on the River Derwent. Everything there was new: machines, clocks, a bell, two 12-hour shifts, hundreds of workers — most of them children, some only seven years old. Arkwright built houses for his workers, and the factory gates shut precisely on the hour. In 1785 a court annulled his patents — Highs and Kay testified that the idea was not his. Arkwright was knighted all the same and became one of the richest men in the country. James Watt's steam engine, patented that same year of 1769, would come to his mills later.
level.cromford_1771.goal: The barber Arkwright gets a machine someone else conceived, the hosiers' money and a river — and builds one of the first modern cotton-spinning mills
level.cromford_1771.hint: The machine is built by the man who knows how, not the man who dreamed it up. A factory is not a spinning wheel at home.
level.cromford_1771.intro: The 1760s, Lancashire. Weavers need more yarn than family spinning wheels can produce. Inventors are wrestling with a machine that could spin strong thread without a spinner. Former barber and wig dealer Richard Arkwright is no great mechanic — but he knows how to find people and money.
level.cromford_1771.source: Richard Arkwright's patent (1769); R. S. Fitton, 'The Arkwrights: Spinners of Fortune' (1989)
level.cromford_1771.title: The Gates of Cromford
level.darwin_1859.fact: Darwin's friends, the geologist Charles Lyell and the botanist Joseph Hooker, found an honourable solution: on July 1, 1858, Darwin's notes and Wallace's paper were read together at the Linnean Society. Neither author was in the room: Wallace was in the Malay Archipelago, and Darwin was burying his infant son. A year and a half later, on November 24, 1859, "On the Origin of Species" came out — and the entire first printing was snapped up by booksellers on the very first day. In June 1860 in Oxford, Bishop Samuel Wilberforce reportedly asked Thomas Huxley whether it was through his grandfather or his grandmother that he claimed descent from an ape; Huxley replied that he would not be ashamed of such an ancestor, but would be ashamed of a man who used his gift of speech to obscure a serious question. Nobody wrote down the exact words. The ailing Darwin did not go to Oxford. And one important point: Darwin never claimed that man descended from apes — in his theory, humans and apes share a common ancestor.
level.darwin_1859.goal: A letter from the Malay islands finally forces Darwin to speak — two men share the discovery, the book comes out, and "Darwin's bulldog" Huxley takes on the bishop
level.darwin_1859.hint: For twenty years the theory lay in a drawer — it took someone else's letter to move it. Darwin himself won't go to Oxford to argue.
level.darwin_1859.intro: 1858. For twenty years Charles Darwin has been gathering evidence that species change through natural selection — and saying nothing. He fears scandal and fears upsetting his deeply religious wife Emma. Then the post brings a paper from a young naturalist, Alfred Wallace, on the island of Ternate: it sets out almost exactly the same theory.
level.darwin_1859.source: Charles Darwin, 'On the Origin of Species' (1859); Francis Darwin (ed.), 'The Life and Letters of Charles Darwin' (1887)
level.darwin_1859.title: On the Origin of Species
level.davison_1913.fact: Suffragettes on hunger strike were force-fed through a tube. In April 1913 Parliament passed a law nicknamed the "Cat and Mouse Act": an emaciated prisoner was released home, and once she recovered she was arrested again — Pankhurst went through this many times. On June 4, 1913, at the Derby at Epsom, Emily Davison stepped onto the track in front of King George V's horse Anmer, was knocked down and died four days later. Whether she meant to die is still debated: a return ticket was found on her, and the newsreel suggests she was trying to fasten a suffragette scarf to the horse. Her funeral became a procession of thousands. That same summer Fawcett's peaceful union held the "Great Pilgrimage": women marched on London from all over the country, tens of thousands gathered for a rally in Hyde Park on July 26, and in August Asquith received their delegation. Women won the vote only in 1918 — and not all of them.
level.davison_1913.goal: 1913: hunger strikes and the "Cat and Mouse Act," Emily Davison's death at the Derby — and a peaceful march after which the Prime Minister hears the suffragists out
level.davison_1913.hint: The movement for the vote has two roads — stones and marches. Whoever walks the peaceful road must not pick up stones.
level.davison_1913.intro: 1913. The women of Britain have been fighting for the vote for half a century. Millicent Fawcett's union works peacefully — petitions, meetings, marches. Emmeline Pankhurst's Women's Social and Political Union has chosen "deeds, not words": it smashes shop windows, sets fire to empty buildings and goes on hunger strike in prison. Prime Minister H. H. Asquith opposes votes for women.
level.davison_1913.source: Emmeline Pankhurst, 'My Own Story' (1914); Prisoners (Temporary Discharge for Ill-Health) Act (1913)
level.davison_1913.title: The King's Horse
level.domesday_1086.fact: According to the "Anglo-Saxon Chronicle," the king "had much thought and very deep discussion" with his council and sent his men into every shire. In each hundred, jurors — Normans and English alike — answered on oath: who held the land under King Edward, who holds it now, how many ploughs, meadows and mills are there and what it is worth. The chronicler fumed that there was "not one ox, nor one cow, nor one pig" left out of the record. It was not a census of people but a survey of land, taxes and feudal rights. The work was apparently compiled into a book by William of St-Calais, Bishop of Durham — though that is historians' reconstruction, not direct testimony. Picot, Sheriff of Cambridge, is called a "hungry lion" and a "prowling wolf" in the monastic chronicle of Ely — for the lands he took from the monks. The English nicknamed the survey "Domesday Book": like the verdict of the Last Judgement, there was no appeal against it.
level.domesday_1086.goal: The Conqueror orders a survey of most of England's land: neighbours say under oath who holds what — and it is all gathered into one book
level.domesday_1086.hint: The truth will come from the jurors, not from the man who seized the land himself. And don't ruin a witness with taxes before he has given evidence.
level.domesday_1086.intro: Christmas 1085, Gloucester. Twenty years ago William of Normandy conquered England and shared out the land among his barons. Now a Danish invasion threatens the country, the army must be fed, and the king doesn't really know what he owns himself or what his barons hold.
level.domesday_1086.source: 'Anglo-Saxon Chronicle', entry for 1085; 'Domesday Book' (1086); 'Book of Ely' (Liber Eliensis, 12th c.)
level.domesday_1086.title: Domesday Book
level.drogheda_1649.fact: On September 10, 1649, Cromwell summoned the town to surrender, and Aston refused. By the laws of war of that era, a garrison that refused to surrender before the walls were breached forfeited its right to quarter. On September 11, after two assaults had been beaten back, the troops burst through the breach, and Cromwell forbade them to spare "any that were in arms." Aston was beaten to death with his own wooden leg — the soldiers thought there was gold hidden inside it. About three thousand defenders died; historians still argue over the number of civilian victims, priests among them. Cromwell wrote to William Lenthall, Speaker of Parliament, that this was "a righteous judgment of God" for the massacre of Protestants in 1641, even though Drogheda had nothing to do with it. A month later a similar slaughter took place at Wexford. The conquest was followed by the confiscation of land from Irish Catholics; in Ireland, Drogheda became a symbol of the cruelty of English rule.
level.drogheda_1649.goal: Ormond leaves Drogheda to hold out, the governor Aston refuses to surrender — and Cromwell takes the town by storm, forbidding quarter
level.drogheda_1649.hint: A town that is meant to be held must first be entrusted to someone. Whoever opens the gates on terms never faces the storm.
level.drogheda_1649.intro: August 1649. Charles I was beheaded half a year ago. In Ireland the Catholic Confederates and the English Royalists under the Marquess of Ormond have joined forces against Parliament. Oliver Cromwell lands at Dublin with an army of veterans. Ormond decides not to meet him in battle but to tie him down with sieges: let the Irish winter and disease do their work. The key to the north is the town of Drogheda, where Ormond has left a Royalist governor, Sir Arthur Aston.
level.drogheda_1649.source: Oliver Cromwell's letter to Speaker William Lenthall (September 17, 1649); Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, 'The History of the Rebellion'
level.drogheda_1649.title: Drogheda
level.easter_1916.fact: On Easter Monday, April 24, 1916, some sixteen hundred rebels seized buildings in central Dublin, and Pearse read out the Proclamation of the Irish Republic outside the General Post Office. Most Dubliners did not support the Rising. British artillery smashed the city centre; on April 29, to stop the killing of civilians, Pearse surrendered unconditionally — the surrender was accepted by Brigadier-General Lowe. From then on everything was decided by General John Maxwell: closed courts martial and, from May 3 to 12, fourteen executions by firing squad in Kilmainham Gaol. The badly wounded Connolly was shot tied to a chair. Markievicz, who had fought at St Stephen's Green, had her death sentence commuted to life "solely and only on account of the prisoner's sex." The executions turned public opinion: two years later Sinn Féin swept away the Irish Parliamentary Party, and the road led to the War of Independence of 1919–1921 and the partition of the island.
level.easter_1916.goal: At Easter 1916 Pearse and Connolly proclaim a republic and surrender six days later — and General Maxwell's firing squads turn defeat into the beginning of a new Ireland
level.easter_1916.hint: No one who agreed to wait will proclaim a republic. The general holds only one court, but its sentences differ.
level.easter_1916.intro: April 1916. The Home Rule Act was passed back in 1914 but suspended until the end of the war, and John Redmond, leader of the Irish Parliamentary Party, is urging the Irish to fight for Britain. A small group — the poet and teacher Patrick Pearse, the socialist James Connolly with his Citizen Army, Countess Constance Markievicz — believes they cannot wait: while Britain is at war, the time to rise is now.
level.easter_1916.source: Proclamation of the Irish Republic (1916); court-martial records, May 1916
level.easter_1916.title: The Dublin Post Office
level.edington_878.fact: In spring Alfred came out of the marshes to Egbert's Stone and called out the levy — the fyrd — of Somerset, Wiltshire and Hampshire; the chronicle says the men "rejoiced to see him." A little earlier, Odda, ealdorman of Devon, had defeated another Viking band in the west and captured their raven banner. At Edington the English routed the Danes and then besieged Guthrum for two weeks until he surrendered. Alfred did not execute his enemy: Guthrum was baptized under the name Æthelstan, with the king as his godfather. A later treaty divided England: the north-east became the Danelaw. Alfred built fortified towns — burhs — and a fleet. And the story of the cakes the king burned in a swineherd's hut is a later legend, written down about a hundred years afterwards.
level.edington_878.goal: The king who hid in the marshes musters the levy, defeats the Danes at Edington and baptizes their leader
level.edington_878.hint: You can't bring an army out of the marshes — you have to call it. A dead enemy signs no peace: Alfred needs a godson, not a head.
level.edington_878.intro: January 878. Just after Twelfth Night the Danish leader Guthrum launched a surprise attack on the royal estate at Chippenham. Wessex — the last English kingdom not conquered by the Vikings — fell within days. King Alfred and a handful of men are hiding on the marshy island of Athelney in Somerset.
level.edington_878.title: Out of the Marshes
level.famine_1845.fact: Prime Minister Robert Peel secretly bought £100,000 worth of maize in America and pushed through the repeal of the Corn Laws, but in June 1846 his government fell. The new cabinet of Lord John Russell and the Treasury official Charles Trevelyan believed the state must not interfere with the market: grain and livestock kept being shipped out of Ireland, and relief came through public works, where starving people built roads to nowhere for a pittance. In spring 1847 free soup kitchens fed up to three million people a day, but by autumn they were closed and relief was shifted onto the local poor rate. Under the "Gregory clause," any tenant holding more than a quarter of an acre lost the right to poor-law relief, especially outside the workhouse — families gave up their land, and landlords tore down their cabins. Between 1845 and 1852 about a million people died, and more than a million left for America and Britain, many on overcrowded "coffin ships." Trevelyan wrote of the famine as a "direct stroke of an all-wise and all-merciful Providence"; John Mitchel, transported in 1848, replied that God had sent the potato blight, but the English had made the famine. Historians still argue over how much the government was to blame, but they agree: policy turned a crop failure into a catastrophe.
level.famine_1845.goal: The potatoes rot three years running, the government relies on the market and the Poor Law — and a million Irish leave across the ocean
level.famine_1845.hint: The potato blight is only the beginning: it's the men in London who decide. As long as Peel's maize feeds the people, history runs differently.
level.famine_1845.intro: 1845. A third of the Irish live almost entirely on potatoes grown on tiny rented patches of land. In autumn a disease arrives from America — blight — and the tubers rot right in the ground. Since 1801 Ireland has been part of the United Kingdom, and decisions about relief are made in London.
level.famine_1845.source: Charles Trevelyan, 'The Irish Crisis' (1848); John Mitchel, 'The Last Conquest of Ireland (Perhaps)' (1861)
level.famine_1845.title: The Great Famine
level.felton_1628.fact: In June 1628 Charles I, desperate for money, accepted the Petition of Right: no taxes without Parliament's consent, no arrest without cause shown, no billeting of soldiers in private houses and no martial law in peacetime. Straight afterwards the Commons addressed a remonstrance to the king naming Buckingham as the cause of all the kingdom's ills. Lieutenant John Felton — wounded at Ré, passed over for promotion and left unpaid — read the remonstrance, bought a knife, and on August 23, 1628, at the Greyhound Inn in Portsmouth, stabbed the duke in the chest. Crowds in the streets drank his health; Felton was hanged at Tyburn. The murder was not "revenge for the Petition," but it grew from the same hatred of the favourite. In 1629 Charles dissolved Parliament and ruled without it for eleven years, and Eliot died in the Tower in 1632.
level.felton_1628.goal: Parliament wrings the Petition of Right from Charles I, and an aggrieved officer, fired up by speeches against the favourite, murders Buckingham
level.felton_1628.hint: The assassin needs a grievance of his own — and the duke himself provides it. And don't send the speaker to the Tower before he has had his say.
level.felton_1628.intro: 1628. George Villiers, Duke of Buckingham, the all-powerful favourite of two kings, bungles one war after another: in 1627 his landing on the French island of Ré ended in disaster. To raise money, Charles I levies a "Forced Loan" and jails those who refuse without trial. Parliament, led by Sir John Eliot, refuses to grant money until the king recognizes the rights of his subjects.
level.felton_1628.source: The Petition of Right (1628); Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, 'The History of the Rebellion'
level.felton_1628.title: Felton's Blow
level.godiva.fact: The legend goes that Godiva took her husband at his word. She let down her long hair, which covered her to the knees, and rode on horseback through the market square. Out of respect for her, the townsfolk closed their shutters and stayed indoors. The earl kept his word and freed Coventry from the tolls. Later versions added Tom the tailor: he alone bored a hole in his shutter, peeped — and was struck blind; hence the English phrase "peeping Tom." Godiva herself was real: she and Leofric founded a monastery in Coventry in 1043 and gave generously to churches. But the ride is first mentioned by chroniclers of the 13th century, some century and a half after her death.
level.godiva.goal: The countess accepts her husband's mocking condition and rides through Coventry to free the townsfolk from the tax
level.godiva.hint: The earl sets a condition — it has to be heard first. And at that hour the square must be empty: the curious have no place there.
level.godiva.intro: Coventry, 11th century. Leofric, Earl of Mercia, has laid a heavy tax on the town. His wife Godiva begs him again and again to spare the townsfolk. Weary of her pleas, the earl snaps: "Ride naked through the market — then I'll lift it."
level.godiva.title: Lady Godiva
level.home_rule_1886.fact: In December 1885 Gladstone's son Herbert let slip his father's views to journalists — the "Hawarden Kite." Parnell backed Gladstone, and he became Prime Minister again. In March 1886 the Radical Joseph Chamberlain resigned from the government in protest, while the Conservative Lord Randolph Churchill decided to "play the Orange card" — to play on the fears of Ulster's Protestants; his phrase "Ulster will fight, and Ulster will be right" became a slogan. On April 8 Gladstone introduced the bill, and on June 8 the House rejected it by 343 votes to 313: 93 Liberals voted against. The party split, and the breakaway Liberal Unionists went over to the Conservatives. A second bill passed the Commons in 1893 but was thrown out by the Lords; a third became law in 1914 — and was suspended because of the war. The dispute over whether to include Ulster ended with the partition of the island in 1921.
level.home_rule_1886.goal: Gladstone allies with Parnell and introduces a bill for Irish self-government — but the bill is killed not by the Tories but by a split in his own party
level.home_rule_1886.hint: The bill was sunk not by the Prime Minister's enemies but by his own allies. Guard the alliance with the Irish to the end — a concession behind their backs will break it.
level.home_rule_1886.intro: Late 1885. At the election Charles Stewart Parnell's Irish party won 86 seats and holds the balance in the Commons: neither Liberals nor Conservatives can govern without it. Ireland demands Home Rule — its own parliament in Dublin. The 76-year-old Liberal William Gladstone has long believed there is no other way to govern Ireland. But his party thinks otherwise.
level.home_rule_1886.source: Government of Ireland Bill (1886); House of Commons debates (Hansard), April–June 1886
level.home_rule_1886.title: Home Rule
level.india_1857.fact: The new Enfield rifles were loaded with cartridges whose paper had to be bitten open — and a rumour spread that it was greased with cow and pig fat, defiling Hindus and Muslims alike. In March the sepoy Mangal Pandey attacked his officers at Barrackpore and was hanged. On May 10 at Meerut, sepoys whose comrades had been put in irons for refusing the cartridges rose up, killed officers and Europeans, and by morning were in Delhi, where they proclaimed Bahadur Shah head of the uprising. Awadh, Cawnpore and Jhansi rose. At Cawnpore, Nana Sahib's men massacred the British garrison after it surrendered, and then, at the Bibighar, some two hundred women and children. British troops took revenge no less brutally: they hanged villagers without trial, blew prisoners from cannon, and after storming Delhi in September looted and killed its inhabitants. The Governor-General, Lord Canning, tried to restrain the vengeance — and earned the scornful nickname "Clemency Canning." Rani Lakshmibai fell in battle in June 1858; Bahadur Shah was tried and exiled to Rangoon, and his sons were shot. In August 1858 Parliament transferred India from the Company to the Crown, and Canning became the first Viceroy. In Britain these events were long called the "Sepoy Mutiny"; in India they are called the Revolt of 1857 or the First War of Independence.
level.india_1857.goal: A rumour about cartridges sets the sepoys rising, they proclaim the last Mughal — the revolt is crushed, and India passes from the Company to the British Crown
level.india_1857.hint: One man's shot won't raise an army — a rumour will. Mercy promised too early will stop history in its tracks.
level.india_1857.intro: 1857. Most of India is ruled not by the British state but by the East India Company, a trading company with its own army — nearly three hundred thousand Indian soldiers, the sepoys, and some forty thousand Britons. The Company annexes princely states whose rulers have no blood heir and meddles in customs and faith. In Delhi there still lives an old poet, Bahadur Shah Zafar — the Mughal Emperor, left with nothing but a title and a palace.
level.india_1857.source: William Dalrymple, 'The Last Mughal' (2006); Government of India Act (1858)
level.india_1857.title: Delhi and Cawnpore
level.lamps_1914.fact: Germany supplied the reason. Under the Schlieffen Plan its army was to march on France through Belgium, and Britain had guaranteed Belgian neutrality by the treaty of 1839. On August 2 Germany demanded passage for its troops; on August 3 Grey spoke in the Commons, and the wavering ministers, Lloyd George among them, stayed in the government — only two resigned. As early as August 1, King George V and his cousin Kaiser Wilhelm II had exchanged telegrams over a misunderstanding that France was ready to stay neutral — it did not delay the war. On August 4 German troops entered Belgium, Britain demanded their withdrawal, and at 11 p.m. London time the ultimatum expired. In his memoirs Grey recalled telling a friend on the evening of August 3, as he watched the lamps being lit: "The lamps are going out all over Europe." The war had no single cause: alliances, the naval race, mobilizations and the general staffs' calculations all came together.
level.lamps_1914.goal: Germany marches through Belgium, Grey's speech holds the cabinet together, and the British ultimatum expires at eleven at night on August 4
level.lamps_1914.hint: The cabinet stays divided until something happens that can be named in the House. Family telegrams can no longer stop the war.
level.lamps_1914.intro: Early August 1914. Austria is at war with Serbia; Russia and Germany have mobilized. Britain is bound to France and Russia by friendship but not by treaty, and half of Asquith's Liberal cabinet opposes war — among the doubters is the Chancellor of the Exchequer, David Lloyd George. The Foreign Secretary, Sir Edward Grey, is searching for an argument everyone will understand.
level.lamps_1914.source: Edward Grey, 'Twenty-Five Years' (1925); Treaty of London on Belgian neutrality (1839)
level.lamps_1914.title: The Lamps Go Out
level.llywelyn_1282.fact: On Palm Sunday 1282 Dafydd made a surprise attack on the English castle of Hawarden, and Wales rose; Llywelyn joined his brother. John Pecham, Archbishop of Canterbury, tried to negotiate and passed on the terms: the prince would receive an estate in England worth a thousand pounds a year if he gave up Wales. Llywelyn refused, replying that his people would not give up their land and their customs. On December 11, 1282, near the bridge at Cilmeri, he broke away from his army with a small band and was killed by an English soldier who did not know whom he was killing. The prince's head was taken to London and displayed on the Tower. Dafydd was captured in the summer of 1283; at Shrewsbury he was tried and executed as a traitor — hanged, drawn and quartered. The Statute of Rhuddlan of 1284 imposed English rule on Wales, and the castles of Conwy, Caernarfon and Harlech rose along the coast. Edward's son received the title "Prince of Wales" only in 1301. In Wales Llywelyn is called "the Last," and his death marks the end of independence.
level.llywelyn_1282.goal: The brothers' rising of 1282 ends with Llywelyn's death at Cilmeri and Dafydd's execution — Wales loses its independence
level.llywelyn_1282.hint: The younger brother starts the rising, the elder follows. A man who has taken an estate in England will never come to the bridge.
level.llywelyn_1282.intro: 1282. Llywelyn ap Gruffudd is the only Welsh ruler the English Crown has ever recognized as "Prince of Wales." But after the war of 1277 King Edward I took half his lands, and in what remains English officials try Welshmen under English law. The prince's younger brother Dafydd, who once fought on the English side himself, holds the bitterest grudge against the king.
level.llywelyn_1282.source: 'Chronicle of the Princes' (Brut y Tywysogion); letters of Archbishop Pecham (1282); Statute of Rhuddlan (1284)
level.llywelyn_1282.title: The Last Prince of Wales
level.luddites_1812.fact: The Luddites did not smash just any machinery, but the machines of masters who cut wages and threw skilled men out of work — and at first they shed no blood. In February 1812 the young Byron spoke in the House of Lords against the bill, and in March Parliament made frame-breaking a capital crime. In April a young cropper, George Mellor, led more than a hundred men against William Cartwright's mill at Rawfolds — it was guarded by soldiers, and two of the attackers died. Two weeks later the mill owner William Horsfall, who had vowed to "ride up to his saddle girths in Luddite blood," was shot on the road across Crosland Moor. For six months the killers could not be found, until an accomplice, Benjamin Walker, turned King's evidence in exchange for a pardon. In January 1813 a Special Commission at York sentenced Mellor and his comrades Thorpe and Smith — they were hanged on January 8, and over the following days fourteen more men. Ned Ludd himself, the legendary apprentice who smashed a stocking frame, most likely never existed.
level.luddites_1812.goal: Yorkshire croppers smash the machines taking away their work — despair drives them to murder a mill owner, and the state answers with the gallows
level.luddites_1812.hint: An attack on the mill settles nothing. The York court is powerless without a witness — and a witness bound by an oath stays silent.
level.luddites_1812.intro: 1812, West Yorkshire. The war with Napoleon is on, trade has ground to a halt, and bread is dear. The croppers — the most skilled workers in the woollen trade — watch new shearing frames make their craft redundant. At night masked bands smash the machines with hammers and sign their letters with the name of "General Ned Ludd."
level.luddites_1812.source: E. P. Thompson, 'The Making of the English Working Class' (1963); report of the trials before the Special Commission at York (1813)
level.luddites_1812.title: Night of the Frame-Breakers
level.matilda_1142.fact: The siege dragged on for almost three months, and food in the castle was running out. In December 1142 snow fell and the Thames froze. According to the "Gesta Stephani," Matilda and three or four knights climbed down from the wall at night and, in white cloaks that blended with the snow, crossed the ice past the king's sentries, then made their way on foot to Abingdon and Wallingford. There she was met by the returning Robert of Gloucester. A year earlier she had already fled from Winchester, and in that same year of 1141 Stephen himself had spent time as her prisoner. Matilda never won the crown: under the Treaty of Winchester in 1153, Stephen recognized her son as his heir — the future Henry II, first of the Plantagenets.
level.matilda_1142.goal: Besieged in Oxford, Empress Matilda escapes across the ice of the frozen Thames — and finds refuge with her own people
level.matilda_1142.hint: You can only escape from a siege. And on the far bank, trust the one who has never changed sides.
level.matilda_1142.intro: 1142, England in "the Anarchy." The old king Henry I left the throne to his daughter Matilda, widow of the German emperor and now wife of the Count of Anjou, but the crown was seized by her cousin Stephen of Blois. For years the barons have fought now for one, now for the other. Stephen's brother, Henry, Bishop of Winchester, went over to Matilda and back again. Her half-brother Robert of Gloucester has sailed to Normandy for help — and meanwhile Stephen has besieged Matilda in Oxford Castle.
level.matilda_1142.source: 'Gesta Stephani' (The Deeds of Stephen, 12th c.); Henry of Huntingdon, 'Historia Anglorum'
level.matilda_1142.title: Night on the Ice
level.montfort_1265.fact: On May 14, 1264, at Lewes, Montfort defeated the royal army and captured Henry III and his son Edward. He had to govern in the captive king's name, and in January 1265 Montfort summoned a parliament to which, besides the barons and prelates, came two knights from each shire and — the great innovation — two burgesses from selected towns. This was not yet democracy: Montfort was looking for support against hostile barons. In May Edward suggested his guards hold horse races, wore out their horses and galloped off to Roger Mortimer. On August 4, 1265, at Evesham, he trapped Montfort's army in a loop of the River Avon. A chronicler called it "murder, not battle": Montfort was cut down and his body mutilated. Henry III himself was in Montfort's army — wounded, he saved himself by crying out: "I am Henry of Winchester, your king!" The parliament with representatives of the towns outlived its creator.
level.montfort_1265.goal: Simon de Montfort takes the king prisoner and summons townsmen to Parliament — but six months later the escaped Prince Edward kills him at Evesham
level.montfort_1265.hint: Parliament must be summoned while the king is a captive and the earl is alive. The prince needs a helper to escape — and no oaths before that.
level.montfort_1265.intro: 1264. King Henry III squanders money on foreign adventures and hands out offices to his wife's relatives. The barons, led by his brother-in-law Simon de Montfort, Earl of Leicester, demand that the king rule together with a council — as laid down in the Provisions of Oxford of 1258. The king refuses, and war breaks out.
level.montfort_1265.source: 'Chronicle of Robert of Gloucester' (late 13th c.); William Rishanger, 'Chronicle'; writs of summons to the Parliament of 1265
level.montfort_1265.title: The Commons' First Voice
level.naseby_1645.fact: Rupert struck the left wing of the Parliamentarian horse and routed it, but his riders galloped after the fugitives all the way to the baggage train and came back only when it was all over. On the other flank Cromwell smashed Langdale's cavalry and, holding his "Ironsides" back from the chase, wheeled them against the king's infantry. When the king wanted to lead the reserve himself, the Earl of Carnwath seized his horse's bridle, asking "Will you go upon your death?" — and the reserve fell back. The king's foot were killed or surrendered. In the abandoned baggage train Charles's private correspondence was found: he had been seeking troops from the Irish Catholics and help from foreign princes. Parliament printed it under the title "The King's Cabinet Opened," and many waverers turned against the king. Naseby did not make England a republic overnight — Charles's trial was still three and a half years away.
level.naseby_1645.goal: Prince Rupert gallops off after the fugitives, Cromwell's disciplined cavalry decides the battle of Naseby — and the king's letters are found in the baggage train
level.naseby_1645.hint: A brilliant charge can be worse than a failure if no one comes back from it. The letters go to the victor, not to whoever goes looking for them.
level.naseby_1645.intro: June 14, 1645, Naseby. The Civil War between King Charles I and Parliament is in its third year. Parliament has just created the "New Model Army": a professional force with regular pay, where command goes by merit, not birth. Its commander is Sir Thomas Fairfax; Oliver Cromwell leads the cavalry of the right wing. The king has the finest cavalryman of the age, his nephew Prince Rupert of the Rhine.
level.naseby_1645.source: 'The King's Cabinet Opened' (1645); Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, 'The History of the Rebellion'
level.naseby_1645.title: Papers in the Coach
level.peterloo_1819.fact: On August 16, 1819, some 60,000 people gathered on the field. The columns marched with bands and banners reading "Reform" and "No Corn Laws"; Samuel Bamford, a weaver and poet from Middleton, led his neighbours in with "cleanliness, sobriety, order," without sticks. The day before, Hunt had offered to give himself up to the magistrates, but was told there was no warrant. When he mounted the platform, the magistrates, led by William Hulton, ordered his arrest; the Manchester and Salford Yeomanry — local shopkeepers and masters on horseback — hacked into the crowd, followed by the hussars. Within ten minutes the field was empty: about 18 people were killed and between 400 and 700 wounded, women and children among them. A newspaper dubbed the massacre "Peterloo" — in mockery of Waterloo. The Home Secretary, Lord Sidmouth, passed on the Prince Regent's thanks to the magistrates, and in December Parliament passed the "Six Acts" against public meetings and the radical press. Hunt got 30 months in prison, Bamford a year. Electoral reform would come only in 1832.
level.peterloo_1819.goal: Sixty thousand peaceful people come to Manchester to ask for reform — the cavalry answers with sabres, and the government thanks the magistrates
level.peterloo_1819.hint: The strength of this crowd is that it is unarmed. And the speaker belongs on the platform, not in a cell.
level.peterloo_1819.intro: 1819, Manchester. A city of cotton mills with almost a hundred thousand people sends not a single member to Parliament, and only a small share of adult men can vote. After the Napoleonic Wars bread is dear and weavers' wages are falling. The Radicals call the people to St Peter's Field to hear the famous orator Henry Hunt.
level.peterloo_1819.source: Samuel Bamford, 'Passages in the Life of a Radical' (1844); testimony at Hunt's trial at York (1820)
level.peterloo_1819.title: Peterloo
level.principia_1687.fact: To Halley's question Newton answered at once: "An ellipse" — he had worked it out long ago, but couldn't find his papers and promised to send the calculation. Three months later the treatise "De motu" arrived, and in 1686 the manuscript of the "Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy." The Royal Society had just spent its money on Willughby's lavish "History of Fishes," so Halley printed the "Principia" at his own expense. Then Hooke demanded recognition that he had been first to think of the inverse-square law. Newton flew into a rage, threatened to suppress the third book, "On the System of the World," and struck nearly every mention of Hooke from the manuscript; Halley had to coax him round by letter. In July 1687 the "Principia" came out — with the laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation. Newton had made his great discoveries back in the plague years of 1665–1666, and the story of the apple is a tale he told late in life that became a legend. Flamsteed would later quarrel with Newton over his observations of the Moon.
level.principia_1687.goal: Halley asks Newton about orbits and pays for the printing himself — and the world gets the law of universal gravitation
level.principia_1687.hint: Without the visitor's question the book won't begin, and without money it won't come out. A quarrel over priority before printing could cost an entire book.
level.principia_1687.intro: January 1684. In a London coffee house three Fellows of the Royal Society — Robert Hooke, the architect Christopher Wren and the young astronomer Edmond Halley — are arguing: if gravity weakens with the square of the distance, what curve will a planet follow? Hooke boasts that he knows the answer but won't show it. In August Halley travels to Cambridge to see the reclusive professor of mathematics, Isaac Newton.
level.principia_1687.source: Isaac Newton, 'Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica' (1687); Newton–Halley correspondence (1686)
level.principia_1687.title: The Principia
level.putney_1647.fact: The Putney Debates began on October 28, 1647, and the army's secretary, William Clarke, took them down almost word for word. Colonel Thomas Rainsborough declared: "The poorest he that is in England hath a life to live, as the greatest he" — and therefore must consent for himself to the government he lives under. Henry Ireton, Cromwell's son-in-law, replied that only those with a "permanent fixed interest" in the kingdom — land or membership of a trading corporation — could have a vote; otherwise the poor would vote against property. Cromwell tried to reconcile the two sides. Even the Levellers did not propose votes for women, servants or paupers. On November 11 the king escaped from Hampton Court and the debates were broken off, and on November 15 at Corkbush Field near Ware Cromwell personally quelled regiments that had turned out with the text of the "Agreement" in their hats; one ringleader, Private Richard Arnold, was shot. Britain would get universal male suffrage only in 1918.
level.putney_1647.goal: Leveller soldiers demand a sweeping extension of the male vote, the generals want to keep it mainly for property owners, and the debate ends in mutiny and a firing squad
level.putney_1647.hint: Without the agitators' draft there's nothing to debate. Win them over too soon and there will be no debate at all; crush them only after it.
level.putney_1647.intro: Autumn 1647. The New Model Army has won the war and holds the king prisoner, but Parliament won't pay the soldiers and wants to disband the army. The regiments have elected their own "agitators." The most radical of them, the Levellers, have brought a draft "Agreement of the People": power belongs to the people, Parliament is re-elected every two years, and every man has a vote. The generals convene the army council in St Mary's Church at Putney.
level.putney_1647.source: Records of the Putney Debates, 'The Clarke Papers'; 'An Agreement of the People' (1647)
level.putney_1647.title: Putney: Voices in the Church
level.robin_hood.fact: The ballads tell how, on a narrow log across a stream, Robin met a giant who knocked him into the water in a fight with staves. Robin laughed and invited the strongman to join his band; the giant's name was John Little, and the outlaws jokingly renamed him Little John. Robin came to the sheriff's contest in disguise — in rags, with a patch over one eye. He put his arrow dead in the centre, received the golden arrow from the sheriff's own hands and left unrecognized. Afterwards he shot an arrow to the sheriff with a note: the prize had been taken by Robin Hood. The first ballads of Robin were written down in the 15th century; King Richard, Maid Marian and "rob the rich, give to the poor" were added later. People are still searching for the real Robin — no candidate is beyond dispute.
level.robin_hood.goal: Robin Hood finds a loyal friend in a giant and wins the contest the sheriff arranged to catch him
level.robin_hood.hint: The contest is bait: the sheriff will know England's best archer by his face. And in Sherwood, friends are found in a fight.
level.robin_hood.intro: Sherwood Forest. For years the Sheriff of Nottingham has hunted the outlaw Robin Hood, who robs rich abbots and gives to the poor. Catching him in the forest is impossible — so the sheriff devises a trick: an archery contest with a prize of an arrow of pure gold. Surely England's finest archer won't be able to resist.
level.robin_hood.source: Ballad 'Robin Hood and the Golden Arrow'; 'A Gest of Robyn Hode' (c. 1500)
level.robin_hood.title: The Golden Arrow
level.somme_1916.fact: From June 24 to July 1 British guns fired about a million and a half shells, but many were shrapnel or duds, the wire was left intact in many places, and the German infantry waited it out in dugouts up to ten metres deep. On July 1 at 7:30 a.m. the British went over the top, in many places in neat, walking lines. The machine-gunners climbed out before the attackers could reach them. In a single day the British Army lost 57,470 men, about 19,000 of them killed — the bloodiest day in its history. Lieutenant Siegfried Sassoon watched the attack from the trenches near Fricourt and recorded what he saw in his diary; a year later he would publicly protest against the continuation of the war. Tanks first went into action on the Somme only on September 15. The battle lasted until November and cost all sides more than a million killed and wounded. Historians still argue about Haig, but the army learned from these mistakes — by 1918 it was fighting in a completely different way.
level.somme_1916.goal: A week of shelling, faith that the wire has been cut, and an attack at walking pace — the first day of the Somme becomes the bloodiest day in the British Army's history
level.somme_1916.hint: Shells can't reach men who are deep underground. There are no tanks yet by summer, and the ally at Verdun needs help now.
level.somme_1916.intro: Summer 1916. At Verdun the Germans are grinding down the French army, and the Allies decide to strike on the River Somme. Commander-in-Chief Douglas Haig and Fourth Army commander Henry Rawlinson are preparing an unprecedented bombardment. Many of the soldiers are volunteers of the "Pals battalions": whole streets and factories signed up together. Facing them is General Fritz von Below's Second Army, long since dug deep into the chalk.
level.somme_1916.source: Siegfried Sassoon, 'Memoirs of an Infantry Officer' (1930); British Official History of the War, 'Military Operations: France and Belgium, 1916'
level.somme_1916.title: The First Day on the Somme
level.two_bells_1918.fact: On February 6, 1918, the Representation of the People Act gave the vote to all men from 21 and to women from 30, provided they or their husbands met a property qualification — about 8.4 million women. The age threshold was chosen so that women would not become a majority of the electorate. Millicent Fawcett called the day the act passed the greatest of her life. On November 11 at 5:12 a.m., in Marshal Foch's railway carriage in the Forest of Compiègne, a German delegation led by Matthias Erzberger signed the armistice; at 11 o'clock the guns fell silent. Kaiser Wilhelm II had already abdicated and left for the Netherlands. A November act allowed women to stand for Parliament, and at the election of December 14, 1918, the first woman elected to the House of Commons was Constance Markievicz — she was in Holloway prison and, as a Sinn Féin member, did not take her seat. The first woman to enter the House was Nancy Astor in 1919, and women won the vote on equal terms with men only in 1928.
level.two_bells_1918.goal: 1918 rings twice: women over thirty get the vote, the armistice is signed in the Forest of Compiègne — and the first election open to women sends the first woman to the Commons
level.two_bells_1918.hint: Half a victory is better than none: demanding "everything at once" will wreck the compromise. It isn't the Kaiser who signs the armistice — he has already fled.
level.two_bells_1918.intro: 1918, the last year of the war. For four years millions of women have worked in factories, hospitals and transport — and arguing over whether they are "ready" for the vote has become impossible. The suffragettes called off their campaigns back in 1914. Prime Minister David Lloyd George is leading the country to victory, and the Speaker's Conference is looking for a compromise the House will accept.
level.two_bells_1918.source: Representation of the People Act (1918); Millicent Fawcett, 'The Women's Victory — and After' (1920)
level.two_bells_1918.title: Two Bells
level.union_1707.fact: In 1705 the English Parliament passed the "Alien Act": unless Scotland opened negotiations on union, Scots would be treated as foreigners and their goods barred from England. In three months of 1706, commissioners from the two countries drew up a treaty. Scotland would get 45 seats in the joint House of Commons and 16 peers in the House of Lords, keep its own church, law and schools — and the "Equivalent," £398,085, partly to repay the investors in the Darien scheme. Andrew Fletcher of Saltoun proposed "limitations" on the Crown and an equal partnership instead, but lost. In Edinburgh and Glasgow crowds attacked the houses of union supporters, while £20,000 sent from London was secretly paid out to supporters of union. On January 16, 1707, the Parliament of Scotland ratified the treaty by 110 votes to 69, and on March 25 it met for the last time. Robert Burns would later write: "We're bought and sold for English gold."
level.union_1707.goal: Ruined by Darien and pressed by England, Scotland votes for union in return for promised money — and Great Britain is born
level.union_1707.hint: The stick before the carrot, the carrot before the vote. A royal decree is no substitute for union, and a concession to Fletcher will bury it.
level.union_1707.intro: 1705. The Kingdom of Scotland is ruined: the colony at Darien on the Isthmus of Panama has failed, taking with it, by various estimates, between a quarter and a half of all the country's money. England and Scotland share one queen, Anne, but have separate parliaments. England fears that after the childless Anne dies, the Scots will choose a Catholic king and an alliance with France.
level.union_1707.source: Acts of Union, 1706–1707; Daniel Defoe, 'The History of the Union of Great Britain' (1709)
level.union_1707.title: The Price of Union
level.united_irishmen_1798.fact: At first the society demanded parliamentary reform and equal rights for Catholics; after it was banned it went underground and began preparing a rising with French help. In 1796 Tone brought a French fleet to Bantry Bay, but a storm prevented a landing. The 1798 rising broke out in May: in Wexford, Antrim and Down. Henry Joy McCracken led the rebels against Antrim town, was defeated and hanged in Belfast. Both sides committed atrocities — from the burned barn at Scullabogue to the torture and executions after Vinegar Hill; by various estimates between 10,000 and 30,000 people died. The Lord Lieutenant, Cornwallis, accepted the surrender of General Humbert's French landing force and offered an amnesty to the rank and file. In October Tone was captured aboard a French ship off Lough Swilly; sentenced to hang, he died of a wound he inflicted on himself in his cell. The Chief Secretary, Castlereagh, used peerages and offices to push the Act of Union through the Irish Parliament: on January 1, 1801, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland came into being. George III would not allow the Catholic emancipation that had been promised — and Pitt and Castlereagh resigned.
level.united_irishmen_1798.goal: Tone calls in the French, the 1798 rising is crushed — and London answers with union, abolishing the Irish Parliament
level.united_irishmen_1798.hint: First the alliance of Catholic and Protestant, then the French — and only after defeat, the union. Better not to ask the king about the Catholics in advance.
level.united_irishmen_1798.intro: 1791, Belfast. Ireland has its own parliament, but only Protestants may sit in it, while Catholics — the majority of the country — can neither vote nor stand for election. Inspired by the French Revolution, the Dublin barrister Theobald Wolfe Tone and Belfast Presbyterians found the Society of United Irishmen.
level.united_irishmen_1798.source: 'Life of Theobald Wolfe Tone', edited by his son (1826); Act of Union with Ireland (1800)
level.united_irishmen_1798.title: The United Irishmen
level.whittington.fact: The tale goes: when the merchant fitted out a ship, everyone in the household put something into the venture, and Dick gave the only thing he had — his cat. Running away from London, he sat down on Highgate Hill and heard the bells of Bow Church: "Turn again, Whittington, thrice Lord Mayor of London!" Dick turned back. Meanwhile the ship had put in on the Barbary coast, where the king's palace was overrun with rats; the cat made short work of them, and the king paid a chest of gold for her. Honest Fitzwarren gave it all to Dick, who married his daughter Alice and became Lord Mayor. Richard Whittington was real: a wealthy cloth merchant, he was Mayor of London four times (1397–1419), married Alice Fitzwarin and left money for a hospital, a library and a public latrine by the Thames. The cat, though, appears in stories about him only in the early 17th century.
level.whittington.goal: An orphan sends his only cat to sea, comes back at the call of the bells — and becomes Lord Mayor of London
level.whittington.hint: A runaway never becomes mayor — let him be called back. Fortune will return from overseas if the merchant is honest.
level.whittington.intro: London, around 1380. The orphan Dick Whittington has come from the countryside believing the streets here are paved with gold, and has taken work as a kitchen boy for the merchant Fitzwarren. The cook beats him and rats run about the attic — his only comfort is a cat bought for a penny. In despair, Dick runs away from the city.
level.whittington.source: The play 'The History of Richard Whittington' (1605, lost); Richard Johnson, ballad of Whittington (1612)
level.whittington.title: Whittington and His Cat
level.witan_1066.fact: Edward died on January 5, 1066. According to the "Life of King Edward," before his death he stretched out his hand to Harold and entrusted him with the kingdom and the queen. The council of the great men — the Witenagemot — chose Harold, and on January 6, the very day of Edward's funeral, he was crowned in Westminster Abbey. William declared Harold an oath-breaker: in 1064, having ended up in Normandy, Harold had supposedly sworn on holy relics to support the duke's claim — a scene embroidered on the Bayeux Tapestry. The Pope backed William, and he began building a fleet. Harold's brother Tostig, exiled from Northumbria, urged first the Norman, then the Norwegian, to invade England. So in a single year England had three rival kings — and two battles: at Stamford Bridge and at Hastings.
level.witan_1066.goal: The dying Edward entrusts the kingdom to Harold, the council crowns him — and William of Normandy declares that his crown has been stolen
level.witan_1066.hint: The council makes the king, but first comes the dying man's last word. Meeting the duke before the coronation is dangerous: he holds an oath.
level.witan_1066.intro: Westminster, early January 1066. The childless King Edward the Confessor lies dying beside the new abbey he spent twenty years building. At his bedside is the most powerful man in England, Earl Harold Godwinson. Across the sea two men await their hour: William, Duke of Normandy, to whom Edward, by Norman accounts, had promised the throne, and King Harald Hardrada of Norway.
level.witan_1066.source: 'Vita Ædwardi Regis' (Life of King Edward, c. 1067); 'Anglo-Saxon Chronicle', 1066; William of Poitiers, 'Gesta Guillelmi'
level.witan_1066.title: The Confessor's Crown
level.wycliffe_1382.fact: On May 21, 1382, Courtenay opened a council at the Blackfriars priory in London, and in that very hour an earthquake shook the city. Both sides saw it as a sign: Wycliffe's opponents, that the earth was casting out heresy; Wycliffe himself, that God was angry with the judges. The council condemned 24 of his propositions, and his followers were driven out of Oxford. Wycliffe himself was left alone: he withdrew to his parish of Lutterworth, where he died a natural death in 1384. Back in 1381 Gaunt had come to Oxford and ordered him to keep silent about the Eucharist — Wycliffe did not obey. His followers completed the first full translation of the Bible into English. That year Anne of Bohemia became Queen of England, and Czech students carried Wycliffe's books off to Prague, where Jan Hus read them. In 1428 Wycliffe's bones were dug up, burned and thrown into a river.
level.wycliffe_1382.goal: The archbishop condemns Wycliffe's teaching to the rumble of an earthquake — but his English Bible and books reach Bohemia through scholarly ties between Oxford and Prague
level.wycliffe_1382.hint: The patron who protected him in 1377 orders silence in 1382. The books must exist before anyone can carry them away.
level.wycliffe_1382.intro: 1382. The Oxford theologian John Wycliffe argues that Scripture stands above the Pope, that the Church should not own riches, and that the bread of the Eucharist does not literally become the body of Christ. Five years ago he was shielded by the king's all-powerful uncle, John of Gaunt: his trial at St Paul's ended in a shouting match between the duke and the Bishop of London, Courtenay. But since the Peasants' Revolt of 1381, which some blame on Wycliffe's preachers too, Gaunt has kept his distance. Courtenay is now Archbishop of Canterbury.
level.wycliffe_1382.source: 'Fasciculi Zizaniorum' (Bundles of Tares, 15th c.); Thomas Walsingham, 'Chronicle'
level.wycliffe_1382.title: Wycliffe's Earthquake
level.zong_1781.fact: Over a few days at the end of 1781 the crew of the Zong threw about 130 shackled Africans into the sea; about ten more leapt overboard themselves. When the ship reached Jamaica, it still had water aboard. Collingwood soon died, and the owners claimed £30 from the insurers for each person killed — and in March 1783 a jury at London's Guildhall found in their favour. A few days later Olaudah Equiano, who had himself once been sold into slavery and had bought his freedom, told the abolitionist Granville Sharp about the case. Sharp tried to have the crew tried for murder, but to the authorities this was a matter of property. On appeal in May 1783 Lord Mansfield said the case of the slaves was "the same as if horses had been thrown overboard," but he ordered a new trial: the insurers had shown that water remained. There is no record of a retrial, and no one in the crew was ever punished. But the story of the Zong spread across the country and became one of the movement's arguments: Britain banned the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in the colonies in 1833.
level.zong_1781.goal: Liverpool shipowners claim insurance for murdered captives — and Equiano and Sharp turn the claim into an indictment of the slave trade
level.zong_1781.hint: First the court case over the "cargo," then word reaching the man who can raise an outcry. An English court of 1783 won't take a murder charge head-on.
level.zong_1781.intro: Late 1781. The slave ship Zong, owned by William Gregson's Liverpool syndicate, is carrying more than 440 captives from Africa to Jamaica — twice as many as it can hold. Captain Luke Collingwood has overshot Jamaica, the water is running out, and people are falling sick. Under the insurance, those who die of disease are the owners' loss, but "cargo" thrown overboard to save the ship is paid for by the insurers.
level.zong_1781.source: Gregson v Gilbert (1783); James Walvin, "The Zong: A Massacre, the Law and the End of Slavery" (2011)
level.zong_1781.title: The Zong
